rationale: Scout with a broad organic window to retain early compounds while eluting strongly retained ones. This run will locate the elution window and critical pairs before targeted slope and temperature adjustments.
Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method while retaining the same solvent window and temperature.

Test one further gradient reduction to establish the speed limit at 40 C; the critical pair is slope-sensitive and may fall below baseline resolution. Injection 2 remains a faster method with the maximum CRF if this step sacrifices separation.

Test whether higher temperature restores selectivity for the critical pair while further reducing retention. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect; injection 2 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Higher temperature worsened several separations, so test the low-temperature endpoint at the same gradient slope. This may resolve the critical middle pair while retaining a shorter elution time than the fully resolved 8-minute gradient.

Return to the fully resolving 8-minute gradient and test moderate heating to shorten retention. At 50 C, the temperature trends suggest improved middle-pair separation without the early-pair co-elution seen at 60 C.

Raise the starting organic fraction to reduce time before the first peak while making the gradient slightly shallower. This should shorten the elution window while preserving or improving the critical middle-pair separation; the early pair will be monitored for compression.

Increase starting organic another 0.10 to shorten retention while further reducing gradient steepness. The main risk is compression of the early pair, which still had useful resolution margin in injection 7.

Test a shorter gradient at the fastest fully resolved starting composition. The middle pair has little resolution margin, so this run will establish whether further shortening is viable without changing selectivity.

Test whether a much steeper gradient and lower temperature move the critical middle pair through an elution-order crossover into a resolved regime. This is an exploratory speed test; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed method with CRF 1.000.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to shift middle-pair selectivity, with a longer gradient to improve the late-pair resolution seen in injection 10. Lower temperature should help retain the early peaks despite the stronger starting solvent.

Lower the starting fraction to improve early retention and middle-pair separation, while narrowing the gradient window to moderate the slope of the 6-minute gradient. This targets a fully resolved run near or below injection 8's 3.40-minute last-peak time.

Explore the lower-temperature, higher-starting-organic regime to shift selectivity of the persistent middle pair. The longer, shallower gradient should protect late-pair resolution, while the early peaks will reveal whether the stronger starting solvent is tolerable.

Test whether stronger starting solvent moves the middle pair far enough beyond its selectivity crossover to regain full resolution in a faster run. This exploratory condition risks weak early retention; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Lengthen injection 14's gradient by one grid step to test whether the middle pair reaches R ≥ 1.5 while preserving the other separations. Keep the starting fraction unchanged because the first peak is already nearly unretained.

Test a 5 C temperature reduction around the fastest fully resolved method to measure local selectivity changes. This will show whether cooler operation provides enough middle-pair resolution margin for further gradient shortening.

Trim the gradient endpoint while slightly increasing the slope relative to injection 12, targeting a faster fully resolved run. The last peak previously eluted near 0.50 organic, so a 0.65 endpoint should comfortably cover the elution window.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 8 to add resolution margin, while trimming the unused high-organic portion of the gradient. This targets maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient and substantially less organic solvent.

Test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method to seek a shorter last-peak time. The early pair is the main risk because its resolution decreased with heating, while the middle pair improved modestly.

Raise injection 17's temperature by one step to try to bring its middle-pair resolution above 1.5 while shortening retention. The lower starting organic fraction may protect the early pair better than in injection 19, although that pair remains the main risk.

Preserve injection 8's starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while removing the unused high-organic segment. Since all peaks should elute before the gradient ends, this should retain CRF 1.000 and the approximately 3.40-minute last-peak time with a shorter programmed gradient.

Seek more resolution margin by lowering the starting organic fraction and slightly flattening injection 17's gradient. This should improve both critical pairs while keeping all peaks comfortably within 10 minutes and preserving the maximum CRF.

Lower injection 21's endpoint one step to increase the middle-pair resolution margin while retaining the same short programmed gradient. The previous last peak eluted near 0.49 organic, so 0.55 should still cover the elution window without a prolonged hold.

Test a small slope increase from 0.0875 to 0.0917 organic fraction per minute relative to injection 21, seeking a last-peak time below 3.40 minutes. This probes the narrow resolution boundary; injection 21 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Use the final injection to test a cooler alternative to injection 22, whose resolution margin may accommodate the modest temperature shift while improving early-pair separation. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 21 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method with a trimmed gradient.
